act_descriptions.prologue: Before the heist. Before Dex, before Silverhand, before everything.
act_descriptions.act1: The fall. Waking up with a ghost in your head and forty-eight hours on the clock.
act_descriptions.act2: Running toward something. Or away from it. Hard to tell at this point.
act_descriptions.act3: The point of no return. Night City always takes more than it gives.
act_descriptions.epilogue: Whatever comes after. If anything does.

chapters.narrative: The neon haze of Night City clings to V like a second skin, a constant reminder that survival here is a verb, not a noun. They moved through the underbelly of the city with the precision of a blade and the patience of a predator, eyes sharp on the flicker of a preem signal, the hum of a synthwave beat, the pulse of a deal gone wrong. A bodyguard’s gun was still warm in their hand, a silent testament to the night before—when a wrong turn led to a flatline and a lesson in loyalty. V didn’t ask questions; they just kept moving, a ghost in the chrome, chasing the next hit, the next edge, the next way out. The city didn’t care if you were alone, but it didn’t have to. It just had to be.

V’s breath came in shallow bursts, the kind that only a city this thick could make you learn. They’d just slipped through a back alley of the Arasaka compound, a place where the air tasted like burnt circuitry and the walls whispered of deals buried deep in the dark. A job gone sideways, a client who’d called in a favor, and now V was standing at the edge of something bigger than a paycheck—something that pulsed with the same cold hunger as the city itself. The streets of Night City had always been a map of survival, but tonight, they felt like a warning. V didn’t chase ghosts, but sometimes the ghosts chased you. And when that happened, you didn’t run. You listened.

A preem signal flickered in the distance, a ghost of a deal that never was. V’s fingers twitched, a habit as old as the city itself. They’d been chasing edges all night, but tonight, the edge was a mirror. The Afterlife’s menu was a legend, but V knew what it meant—only the dead got their own drink. And V had a feeling this wasn’t the last time they’d be standing on the line between life and the next hit. The city didn’t care if you were alone, but it didn’t have to. It just had to be. And V? V was already moving.

V’s boots echoed against the concrete, a rhythm older than the city itself. The Arasaka back alley had left more than just a taste of burnt circuitry in the air—it left a question, one that pulsed in the marrow of V’s bones. The Afterlife’s menu was more than a legend now; it was a promise, a flicker of something real in the static of a dying world. Biotechnica’s nutrient security had turned hunger into a commodity, but V knew the real currency here wasn’t food—it was survival, and survival was a game of edges. They didn’t chase ghosts, but sometimes the ghosts chased you, and when that happened, you didn’t run. You listened. And V had a feeling this wasn’t the last time they’d be standing on the line between life and the next hit.

The Afterlife’s menu wasn’t just a legend—it was a debt, and V had just signed the receipt. They’d tracked the signal through the underbelly of the city, where the air was thick with the scent of burnt circuitry and the weight of unspoken promises. A preem broker in the old docks had offered a deal: a cache of biotech credits in exchange for a name, a name that could sink a corpo’s empire. V didn’t ask questions. They didn’t need to. The city had a way of making you choose between survival and silence, and V had already chosen. Now they just had to make sure the silence stayed quiet. The NCPD wouldn’t touch this—no badge, no matter how shiny, could claim a ghost. But the streets? The streets had a different kind of law. And V? V was already moving, one step closer to the edge where the living and the dead met.

The preem signal had gone dark, but the weight of it lingered in V’s skull like a bad choom buzz. They’d tracked it to the old docks, where the air was thick with the promise of deals and the scent of rusted chrome. A broker with a name like ash and a face like a ghost had offered a deal—biotech credits in exchange for a name, a name that could sink a corpo’s empire. V didn’t ask questions. They didn’t need to. The city had a way of making you choose between survival and silence, and V had already chosen. Now they just had to make sure the silence stayed quiet. The NCPD wouldn’t touch this—no badge, no matter how shiny, could claim a ghost. But the streets? The streets had a different kind of law. And V? V was already moving, one step closer to the edge where the living and the dead met.

The docks were a graveyard of deals, and V moved like a ghost through the rusted bones of the place. The broker’s name was ash, but the scent of his desperation was sharp—like burnt chrome and old regrets. V didn’t need to ask why the name was worth a cache of biotech credits; they’d seen it before, in the eyes of men who’d sold their souls for a chance to breathe. The city didn’t care about ghosts, but it did care about the weight of names, and V had learned to carry that weight like a second skin. The broker had given them a lead—something about a data vault buried in the belly of the old refinery. V didn’t need to know how it got there. They just needed to know it was there. And the streets, ever hungry, had already begun to whisper.

The refinery’s belly was a cathedral of rust and static, its halls echoing with the weight of secrets long buried. V moved through the darkness, a shadow with a purpose, their steps guided by the ghost of a name and the flicker of a preem signal. The data vault was there, locked behind a firewall older than the city itself, but the real prize wasn’t the credits—it was the black ICE on Arasaka’s net, a ghost in the matrix that had been waiting for someone to find it. V didn’t need to ask why the name was worth more than gold; they’d seen the way the city swallowed its own. They just needed to make sure the silence stayed quiet, and the streets stayed satisfied. The deal was done, but the weight of it lingered, like a choom buzz in the wrong place. And somewhere, in the dark, the ICE was humming, ready to wake.
